Learn From Every Match

Learn how to analyse your tennis matches, identify performance weaknesses and turn competition experiences into practical training goals that improve your game.

Amir Ardekanian · 6 min read · November 2026

📲This article is also in the appAA Performance · opens without an accountOpen →

Winning a match doesn't mean you played well. Losing doesn't mean you played badly. But every match gives you something useful: information about how you played.

Most players finish a match, think "I need a better forehand" or "I need to get fitter", and go back to training without knowing exactly what to work on. Playing matches isn't enough. You have to learn from them.

Here's a simple process to turn every match into clear training goals. I'll use tennis examples, but it works exactly the same in padel.

Look past the score

First, separate how you played from the final score. Picture two players who both lose.

  • Player A walks off angry, sure they played terribly.
  • Player B notices three things: they struggled with high backhands, made poor choices when pulled wide, and lost focus after unforced errors.

Same result. But Player B has something far more useful: information they can take into training. When you review a match, check four areas.

  • Technical: which shots worked, and which caused problems?
  • Tactical: did you make good decisions? Did your game plan work?
  • Physical: could you keep your movement and intensity up for the whole match?
  • Mental: how did you handle pressure, mistakes and big points?
Remember

Not every missed shot is a technique problem. Maybe you were off balance, picked the wrong shot, got there late or rushed under pressure. Knowing why something happened is worth more than knowing what went wrong.

Find patterns, not single mistakes

One missed forehand doesn't mean you have a forehand problem. Maybe you were moving backwards, got a tough ball or went for a winner that wasn't there.

So don't chase single mistakes. Look for the ones that keep coming back. Ask yourself:

  • Did the same problem happen several times?
  • Did it happen in a particular situation?
  • Was it linked to the opponent, the score or the type of ball?
  • Did it get worse as the match went on?

Here's the difference. "My backhand was bad today" is vague. "I kept missing high balls to my backhand, mostly when I was defending from the baseline" tells you exactly where to start.

In padel it might be high balls coming off the back glass. Same idea: name the shot and the situation.

Tip

Use match stats, a video or your coach's notes if you can. In one study, experienced coaches remembered only about 6 in 10 key moments of a match. Your own memory straight after a match won't be perfect either.

Turn what you saw into a goal

Once you've found a problem that keeps coming back, decide what you want to improve. Sport psychology uses three types of goal.

  • Outcome goals: a result, usually measured against other players, like winning a tournament.
  • Performance goals: a measurable improvement in your own game, like fewer backhand errors.
  • Process goals: the actions that get you there, like keeping good spacing on high backhands.

All three help. Process goals are the most useful day to day, because they're about things you control.

So don't stop at "I want to improve my backhand". Make it specific: "I want to stay balanced on high backhands, hit them with more control and recover to a good court position." Now your training has a direction.

The research

A 2022 review of 27 studies found that setting goals improves sports performance. Process goals had by far the biggest effect. Outcome goals on their own did almost nothing. Goals still have to fit you and what you need.

Take your goal into training

A good goal changes what you actually do on court and in the gym. Four examples:

  • Struggling with high backhands: high-ball feeding, backhand technique and work on getting into position.
  • Poor decisions when pulled wide: decision-making drills that train recovery and shot choice.
  • Fading at the end of matches: tennis-specific conditioning, repeated high-intensity drills and better recovery between points.
  • Getting frustrated after mistakes: a between-point routine, breathing and practice under pressure.

Each problem has a matching fix. But don't assume your first explanation is right. A backhand that breaks down could be technique, fatigue, poor positioning or a bad decision. Your coach can help you work out whether the problem is technical, tactical, physical or mental.

Rule

Pick training that fixes the real problem. Doing more exercises isn't the same as doing the right ones.

Pick one or two priorities

After a match you might find five or six things to fix. Don't work on all of them at once. Choose one or two, based on:

  • Impact: how much does it hurt your performance?
  • Frequency: how often does it happen?
  • Trainability: can you realistically improve it with practice?

If your high backhand keeps breaking down and costs you when you defend, it's a better priority than the odd double fault.

Set a clear goal, pick the right training and track your progress. Then check whether the training is actually making you better.

Use your next match as the test

Training isn't the finish line. What you practise has to show up in matches.

Say your priority was high backhands, and in training you worked on position, balance and shot choice. In your next match, watch for this:

  • Am I spotting high balls earlier?
  • Am I getting into a better position?
  • Am I making better decisions?
  • Am I hitting the shot more consistently?

You can lose that match and still have made real progress. The question is whether you used what you practised, not just whether you won.

Your 10-minute match review

After your next match, take 10 minutes and answer these six questions.

Step 1 — What went well?

Write down two things you did well.

Step 2 — Biggest problems

Name one or two specific problems.

Step 3 — When?

When did they happen? Think about the score, the opponent, the type of ball and the situation.

Step 4 — Why?

What might have caused them? Think technical, tactical, physical and mental.

Step 5 — Priority

Pick the one area that would make the biggest difference to your game.

Step 6 — Action

Write down one specific thing you'll do in training.

Keep your answers. After a few matches you'll start to see patterns you'd never spot from one match.

What did this match teach you?

Every match is a chance to learn, but you don't get better automatically. You look back at how you played, find your weak spots, set goals that mean something and take them into training.

The cycle

Compete → reflect → set a goal → train → compete again → check your progress.

So don't just ask whether you won or lost. Ask yourself: what did this match teach me, and what am I going to do about it?

Based on Williamson et al. (2024, first published 2022), Bird et al. (2024), Kingston and Hardy (1997), Laird and Waters (2008) and Zimmerman (2000).
